title: Cache-binning hit model and TTL governor recommendations
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Goal: Produce a prescriptive set of recommendations and a safe apply/rollback workflow for prefix/KV cache configuration that optimizes cost by balancing batching and caching, increases effective hit-rate, and enforces TTL governance with minimal production risk. This ticket focuses on two deliverables: (1) a probabilistic hit-model for cache binning and cache-key transforms that drives TTL and bucketization decisions; (2) a TTL governor and policy template with safe-apply guardrails and an automated rollback trigger based on observed delta from expected hit-rate and latency budgets.
acceptance_criteria: A probabilistic hit-rate model implemented as a lightweight service or library that can score prefix buckets against historical traces
A TTL governor config prototype that suggests TTL ranges per bucket and produces a canary rollout plan
Automated safety checks: pre-apply simulation, canary monitor, and rollback trigger thresholds documented and codified
Playbook documented with runbook steps and links to dashboards, PRs, and Confluence design doc
Benchmarks showing >=10% cost reduction on at least two representative workloads without violating 99th percentile latency SLOs
proposal: 1) Hit-model: implement a 'cache-binning' approach where prefixes are clustered into ~8-32 bins by usage entropy, prefix length distribution, and reuse distance. The model will ingest sample traces (token-level prefix fingerprints and inter-request delta) and produce per-bin hit-rate curves for candidate TTLs. We will favor an interpretable probabilistic model (Poisson/Weibull for reuse) with a small ML shim to adjust to non-stationary workloads. 2) TTL governor: given a bin's hit curve and a latency/cost objective, the governor recommends a TTL window (min,max) and a suggested default. 3) Key transforms: offer a short list of deterministic transforms (prefix truncation, stable hashing, bucketed suffix) with estimated collision/hitrate trade-offs. 4) Safe-apply: preflight simulation against a replay engine, canary rollout on a small percent of traffic, live monitor that compares real hit-rate/lambda to model expectation, and automated rollback when deviation crosses thresholds. 5) Integration: expose recommendations via the Console Optimize UI, and provide a CLI/PR template for infra teams to apply configs to Dedicated/Private deployments.
rollout_plan: Phase 1: offline model + recommendation engine prototype; validate on 3 internal workloads (search autocomplete, summarization caching, embeddings lookup). Phase 2: implement TTL governor and CLI to generate config diffs; run preflight simulation and dry-run in staging. Phase 3: canary on 2% traffic for one week, monitor hit-rate and 99th latency; if stable, expand to 25% then 100%. Each expansion gated by success criteria in monitoring. All rollouts will include an automated rollback policy tied to both cost regressions and latency SLO violations.
testing_plan:
- Unit tests for hit-model math and key transforms.
- End-to-end replay tests using archived traces from prod (anonymized).
- Load test the TTL governor on a synthetic workload generator with variable request inter-arrival times.
- Canary instrumentation: metric set includes bin-level hit-rate, per-bin cost-per-token, 99th/95th latency, and error-rate.
- Backstop safety test: forced rollback in staging to validate rollback automation.
risks:
- Model mismatch: real access patterns may be non-stationary and break the probabilistic assumptions, producing unexpected cache thrash.
- Over-aggressive TTLs could increase origin load and latency spikes.
- Collision from key transforms can reduce hit-rate for hot prefixes.
- Data privacy: need to ensure prefix traces are anonymized before model training.
- Operational complexity: adding more bins increases management surface — must keep default paths simple for product teams.
metrics: Primary: per-workload cost reduction (%), overall token cost delta, per-bin hit-rate delta, change in origin request rate. Secondary: 99th percentile latency, error-rate, number of automated rollbacks triggered. Baseline measurements will be captured prior to canary and compared hourly during rollouts.
